title: mg/dL vs mmol/L: Glucose, Cholesterol and the US–EU Divide
h1: Clinical lab units — mg/dL and mmol/L
description: Glucose 100 mg/dL = 5.55 mmol/L. Cholesterol 200 mg/dL = 5.18 mmol/L. The conversion factor is different for every analyte — it depends on molecular weight.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: Every clinical analyte has its own mg/dL ↔ mmol/L factor. Rules of thumb like '18' work for glucose only.
body: US labs report clinical analytes in mg/dL; most of the world uses mmol/L. The conversion is not universal — each substance has a different molecular weight, so a different factor.

> Glucose: mg/dL × 0.0555 = mmol/L (MW 180.16)
> Cholesterol: mg/dL × 0.0259 = mmol/L (MW 386.65)
> Triglycerides: mg/dL × 0.0113 = mmol/L (MW 885)
> Creatinine: mg/dL × 88.4 = µmol/L
> Urea (BUN): mg/dL × 0.357 = mmol/L (BUN is expressed as nitrogen, not urea)
Fasting glucose: 70–100 mg/dL (3.9–5.5). Total cholesterol optimal: <200 (5.18). Triglyceride normal: <150 (1.69). Creatinine adult: 0.6–1.2 (53–106 µmol/L).

A US patient with cholesterol 240 mg/dL sees a European clinician who logs 6.21 mmol/L. Multiply by 39 (wrong — that's glucose's factor for the mg/dL to mmol/L 1/x direction) and you get nonsense. Look up the analyte-specific factor every time.
One conversion per analyte. Do not use glucose's factor for anything else.

faqs.q: Why does BUN use nitrogen mass?
faqs.a: US labs historically measured the nitrogen content of urea. BUN × 2.14 = urea concentration.
Yes — US uses % (NGSP); international uses mmol/mol (IFCC). HbA1c 6.5% ≈ 48 mmol/mol.
